title: I built an AI-powered browser RPG from scratch — new to AI, new to game dev, every mistake possible. Shipped today. Here's the actual dev diary.
author: RepresentativeAd1512
selftext:
**Body:**

I want to be upfront: when I started this project I had never used an AI API, never built a game, and had only a basic grip on web development. Aethermoor: The Chronicles launched today. Here's what the journey actually looked like — the failures included.

**What it is**

A browser-based fantasy RPG where Claude AI acts as a living narrator. Every response, combat outcome, story beat and NPC conversation is generated in real time. There are no pre-written story branches — the world reacts to what you actually do. Four classes, 12 subclasses, a procedurally generated continent, companions, factions, a dungeon, New Game+, 30 achievements, and a token economy for the AI calls.

**Stage 1 — The prototype that shouldn't have worked**

The first version was a single HTML file and a Node.js server.js. The AI call was simple: send the player's last message, get a response, display it. No state tracking, no rules, no game systems. Just vibes.

It worked well enough to be exciting and badly enough to be embarrassing. The AI would:

* Forget the player's name mid-scene
* Invent a new town every time the player moved
* Describe the player teleporting between locations with no travel
* Give the player infinite gold or resurrect dead characters for no reason
* Start every response with "Certainly! Here is your next story beat:"

That last one was the first real lesson: **Claude is not a narrator by default. It's an assistant. You have to teach it to be a narrator.**

**Stage 2 — The system prompt arms race**

This is where most of the actual work happened. Every problem the AI caused became a rule in the system prompt. Some examples:

**The location problem.** The AI would generate a new blacksmith every time the player entered a town — different name, different personality, different location in town. Players noticed immediately. Fix: an ESTABLISHED LOCATION RULE in the prompt. Any named location, business, or NPC that has been introduced is permanent. The AI must reference existing fixtures, never invent replacements.

**The naming problem.** Related — the AI would call the capital city three different things across three turns. Fix: inject all known location names and NPC names directly into the system prompt on every call. Not as context. As law.

**The NPC consistency problem.** Even with names injected, NPCs felt hollow. Fix: generate a name pool seeded from the player's own name and class at world creation. \~50 names, always the same for that player's world. The narrator draws from this pool. Characters feel like they belong to a world rather than being rolled fresh each turn.

**The time problem.** The AI has no concept of in-game time passing. It would describe a journey taking "several days" and then on the next turn act like no time had passed. Fix: track `gameDay` as a hard integer in player state. Inject it into the system prompt as a fact, not a suggestion: `Day: 14`. The narrator is instructed to treat this as the authoritative current day and advance it only when the player explicitly rests or travels long distances.

**The suggestion problem.** The AI would offer the player suggestions like "You could visit the market here in Thornhaven" — even when the player was already standing in Thornhaven's market. It was breaking immersion constantly. Fix: explicit rule — the narrator never suggests the current location as a destination.

**The horse problem.** Players could own horses. The AI kept losing them — describing the player arriving on foot at a stables they'd ridden to. Fix: a dedicated MOUNT line in the state block injected each call, and a HORSE RULE explaining that if the player arrived by horse, the horse is with them. Obvious in hindsight.

None of these are glamorous. Every single one came from a player (or me) noticing something stupid and working backwards to write a rule that stopped it happening.

**Stage 3 — The migration**

The prototype outgrew the prototype. A single server.js file holding all game logic, all AI calls, all routing, and all database queries was becoming impossible to work with. The decision was to migrate to Next.js — full-stack, React frontend, API routes as the backend, PostgreSQL on Railway, deployed on Vercel.

This was painful. Not because Next.js is hard, but because migrating a working (if messy) system to a new architecture while keeping it functional meant touching everything at once.

The biggest migration mistake: not planning the data model first. The original used a flat JSON blob for player state stored in a single column. That's fine for a prototype. For a game with inventory, quests, bestiary, achievements, companions, subclasses, and dungeon state — it became a read/write nightmare. The schema needed to be thought through before migrating, not during.

Lesson: prototype in anything. Ship in a real architecture. Don't try to evolve one into the other without a clean data design first.

**Stage 4 — The streaming problem**

The first version waited for the full AI response before displaying anything. On fast models this was tolerable. On richer models (Sonnet, Opus) the wait was 8-12 seconds of blank screen. Players assumed the game had crashed.

Fix: streaming. The API route now returns `text/event-stream` — the narrative streams to the player token by token like a typewriter. This alone made the game feel alive in a way that nothing else did.

The complication: the game uses structured tags embedded in the AI response to update game state. (`[xp:+50]`, `[gold:-20]`, `[mainQuestAct:2]`, etc.) You can't parse those until the full response arrives. Solution: stream the text display, buffer the full response in parallel for tag parsing, apply state updates only when the stream closes.

**Stage 5 — The save conflict disaster**

Cloud saves use a `saved_at` timestamp to detect conflicts — if the server's saved\_at is newer than what the client sent, there's a conflict. Simple.

Except it wasn't comparing `saved_at`. It was comparing `updated_at`. The narrator updates `updated_at` every single AI call (as it should — it needs to record when state changed). So the conflict check was triggering on every narrator call, not just on actual save conflicts. Players were being told their save was in conflict when they'd done nothing wrong.

This went unnoticed for weeks because during solo testing, the race condition doesn't reproduce reliably. It only showed up clearly during playtesting with multiple simultaneous users.

Fix: one line. Compare `saved_at` vs `saved_at`. Not `updated_at`. Done. Took two minutes to fix, took two weeks to find.

**Stage 6 — Content and pacing**

The AI is genuinely good at creative content. It will happily write a fascinating murder mystery in a village, give the player 45 minutes of side content, and then act confused when the main quest hasn't progressed in a week of real time.

Problem: there was no pacing. The player could stay in the starting town forever. The main quest never pushed.

Fix: act gates. Each act of the main quest requires a minimum number of completed quests and player actions before it can progress. The AI is instructed not to escalate the main story before those gates open. It's blunt but it works — the story moves, the world feels urgent, and players don't soft-lock themselves by ignoring everything.

**Stage 7 — The cost problem**

Running Opus on every call for every player is not sustainable. Early token estimates were badly wrong. Fix: model tier system. Players choose Haiku (1 token/turn), Sonnet (4 tokens/turn), or Opus (20 tokens/turn) from an Options menu. They buy tokens. The AI call routes to the selected model. This gives players control and keeps costs predictable.

Lesson: build cost visibility before you build features. I added admin cost dashboards weeks after launch-ready build and spent a lot of time anxious about numbers I couldn't see.

**Timeline overview**

|Phase|What happened|
|:-|:-|
|Prototype|Single HTML + server.js, basic AI call, no state|
|System prompt v1|Location rules, time tracking, NPC consistency|
|Migration|Next.js, PostgreSQL, full API architecture|
|Streaming|SSE narrative streaming, parallel tag parsing|
|Game systems|Subclasses, companions, dungeon, NG+, achievements|
|Stabilisation|Save conflicts, mobile UX overhaul, cost management|
|Compliance|Cookie consent, age gate, account deletion, moderation|
|Launch|Today — [itch.io](http://itch.io), 50 free tokens for new players|

**What I'd do differently**

* Design the data model before writing a single line of game logic
* Treat the system prompt as code — version control it, test changes against a fixed set of inputs
* Add streaming from day one. It changes everything about feel
* Build cost monitoring before building features
* Playtest with strangers, not friends. Friends are too polite about broken saves and AI weirdness

**Where it is now**

Live at [itch.io](http://itch.io) — [Aethermoor: The Chronicles](https://knoodlepot-game.itch.io/aethermoor-the-chronicles). No download, runs in browser on desktop and mobile. 50 free tokens to start, no payment required to see how it plays.

Happy to answer questions about the AI architecture, the narrator system prompt structure, or anything else in here. This community is where I learned most of what I know — felt right to give something back.

replies.author: tyro12
replies.body:
I understand that you were not in a position to know everything from the start. But it was your responsibility to survey the field before you started making a supposedly competing product. Your attempt to make me feel bad is not working. 

If you figured out Claude, you could have figured out how to ask it what competition is out there. 

"I don't know what that means" is no longer an excuse when we have incredibly intelligent AI models at our fingertips to ask anything we possibly want. 

Ask Claude what I mean by that sentence above. And you'll see that in fact I was quite constructive with my feedback. 

I did in fact check out your game. But as soon as I saw that you plan to resell LLM tokens, I felt grossed out and I knew the whole story already. 

In actual fact I feel quite strongly about this topic because I too am attempting to build an AI-powered storytelling role-playing game sort of system. And I have done extensive research on this area. 

So I'm not gatekeeping. I just told you like it is. You should take this as an opportunity to iterate and improve. 

There's a lot of space in this nascent industry to succeed. But it's not going to happen if you don't allow people to bring their own API keys. 

I'm not going to go and spell everything out that I've learned on my own, because I am in actual fact hoping to be your competition.

replies.author: RepresentativeAd1512
replies.body:

I didn't want to see what the competition has as I wanted to make the game without copying others. I wanted my game with my ideas without influence from others.  
I did this as a fun hobby to get myself out of the shit life I had and it spiralled out of control. Claude coded in VS Code and I told it what to do. I corrected it so many times as it tried to make something it thought I wanted. So I had to make rules in VS Code as well telling Claude off for adding stuff.  
The game took me months to fine tune and build finding 100s of issues and trying to work them out.

replies.author: tyro12
replies.body:
\*sigh\*. 

1. First of all. You should stop using Claude, it's a money sink generally speaking. ChatGPT $20 subscription comes with Codex, which can do quite a bit of coding and gives you subsidized access to some of the best models (GPT 5.5, Codex 5.3). And you can talk to it on the web just as well as you can talk to Claude. Actually, ChatGPT's memory is quite good and it generally knows what you've discussed with it throughout all your chats with it. 

2. If you did not come up on the concept of "Bring Your Own Key" in the space of AI roleplaying, you made serious serious mistakes in what you were asking and how. SillyTavern. Look into it. That's the bare minimum that people want to see when doing AI RP. First question someone who wants to RP will ask is - why don't I just use SillyTavern.   
And now that DeepSeek V4 has come out (particularly the Flash model which is crazy cheap but quite smart still), they will be wondering that even more.

3. Not looking up what the competition is doing is bananas. I understand the idea of not wanting to "poison the well" with external ideas, but that's probably a shit strategy over all, not gonna lie. 

4. I understand that working on this helped you feel better. That's nice. I didn't say anything negative about that part, nor will I. I judged you based on the post and the product only. There's a guy below my comment that just wrote "Dead intetnet theory fr" lol, which is a pretty low effort reply. You will surely admit that I put a fair amount of effort into my comment. Not to mention that, while it was inflammatory and aggressive, certainly, it did also contain some nuggets of useful stuff that you can look into. As well as this further comment. Literally writing a short story's worth of text here in reply to you. 

5. Look into using cheaper models, maybe even multiple at once. Claude is insane as an API provider. Prices are nuts, nobody wants to pay that. Deepseek v4 is a good idea to look into. OR. Like I previously said. Just make a good tool with good features. And let people connect their own AI providers to it. Ask your AI assistants about all this shit I'm saying, they will explain it to you.

replies.author: tyro12
replies.body:
That part was not constructive, nor intended to be. My reaction was as such because there is a slew of very similar services, and I, like many others, have developed an allergic reaction to any kind of roleplaying service which asks you to pay money into it to purchase some kind of "token" to access some giant LLM, with the service acting as a middleman between the user and the actual company running the AI, like OpenAI or Anthropic or whatever else. 

Typically these are shoddily made crap that don't actually bring anything good or innovative to the table. 

Yes, I do think you should "know these things". There's a lot to know, but any AI can help you know them. 

And I was not suggesting multiple subs, I was suggesting replacing Claude with ChatGPT, as its coding offering is superior in terms of value. And also, if you still want to serve as middleman for an LLM API for your potential users, I'd recommend switching to DeepSeek as I said before. It's exponentially cheaper. 

As for the "creatively bankrupt" answer you wrote, supposing that I had no idea what Pokemon is, maybe I grew up under a rock. If I go and publish a game in which you walk around, throw high tech balls at monsters in the grass, imprison them in said balls, then use them to fight other people's monsters, people wouldn't accept me saying "it took me a long time to come up with the idea". 

Also the "dead internet theory" comment was implying that your post was written by an AI, possibly that you yourself as the OP are an AI bot programmed to make these posts. Dead internet theory suggests that a majority of users on the internet in today's day are actually automated bots.

replies.author: Craftybert
replies.body:
Casual observer here, one thing that could help upfront is knowing roughly how many tokens would be needed to complete a run through, i'm guessing there is a logical end to the game, or is it something that you expect people to play indefintely? 

For me, i'm kinda intrigued about this type of thing, reminds me of a more interactive fighting fantasy choose your own adventure book that i enjoyed as a kid. If i knew i could complete a run/campaign in say, 200 tokens or so on the lowest tier, i'd probably chuck a couple of quid at it to see how it is. replies.author: RepresentativeAd1512
replies.body:
For a full run on Haiku to the end is roughly 150-300 tokens depending if you do a little exploring and level up a faction or two. It can take way more ofc if you go to every single POI or settlement. You'll get an end screen with a full summary of what you did.

I hope this answers your question?

replies.author: Craftybert
replies.body: Sounds OKish, I'd suggest putting it on the main page, would entice people in more

comments.author: MongooseEmpty4801
comments.body: TLDR. What makes yours stand out from the dozens of other games exactly like this, and why would someone pay for it?

replies.author: RepresentativeAd1512
replies.body:
I made sure the game had full quest system with 15 templates from which the AI can user to make up stories.  
Text style combat that rewards you if you use flair in the text.  
I added many factions with it's own rewards and quests system.  
Companions you can team up with in game  
I got an infinite dungeon system which adds a leader board so players can see others of how far they got.  
NG+ Carry over with perks to choose and if your player died they can be a boss in the Dungeon.  
30+ Achievements  
The narrator it's self has 100's of rules I had to make from time keeping \*Which took 3 days to resolve for me with no experience)  
I have an evil story arc as well which I think is very good as certain factions side with you and the evil end boss can work with you so the AI changes the dynamic making the Good your enemy.  
I got the map to have coordinates so a mini map shows where you are and if you travel from on place to another due to the cords it'll track time and rations needed and warn you.  
No new game is the same. No map is the same.  
I have jobs like farming, delivery boy, POI's around the world with a mini boss.  
I have pre made a few NPCs with special rules.  
I have a jobs board.  
I made sure the AI remembers where everything is and an NPC tracker with "Last seen"  
The narrator was the most difficult to make as it would hallucinate and make shit up I made sure it had rules to stop that with memory too.

It's not a thin API wrapper.

replies.author: MongooseEmpty4801
replies.body: Does it have a narrative arc, with a beginning, middle and end? Do NPCs go through character development?

replies.author: RepresentativeAd1512
replies.body:
The narrative arc has 5 acts with a central villain, escalating stakes and also three possible endings victory or failure or siding with the darkness. Each handled differently. NPCs can also betray you.

Regarding NPCs they are not where I want them to be but I'm working on that. Full memory would need injecting more context per call. It's a real limitation I need to improve on. And truly I only just thought of this in the last two weeks which I'll hold my hand up I should have thought of that at the start as I always wanted NPCs to work with you.  
The only NPCs with decent memories are my premade ones.

comments.author: MongooseEmpty4801
comments.body: Biggest blocker for me on all of these is I won't buy a game where I don't know how much it's going to cost me. I want a single purchase, not a constant string of micro transactions just to be able to keep playing.
